history.title: Bates Motel
history.review_title: Arguably the greatest show of this century!
history.text: Now that it's all been said and done, BATES MOTEL should go down as one of the greatest TV experiences in history! To be completely honest, I did not in my wildest imagination believe that this season of the iconic series that I'm reviewing, the final one, Season 5, would even be that great. How could it possibly be after Season 4 was so overwhelmingly perfect and at that point the best season the show had ever had?! Boy, was I mistaken! LOL Season 5 somehow, some way, managed to top the superb Season 4 and in doing so, put the ultimate stamp of approval on this already-great series. Unlike most series, the show went out with a bang, not a whimper. Season 5 is definitely the best season of Bates Motel. What were the reasons I was doubtful for Season 5? #1 was no more Norma! At least not the live version. Season 4 ended with Norma's death at the hands of Norman and so in Season 5, we got the Imaginary "Mother" version of Norma that's existed in Norman's mind since early Season 1. But now, ImaginaryNorma is all Norman has. ImaginaryNorma is of course played by the great Vera Farmiga and she did an excellent job of playing the more twisted, no-holds-barred, psychotic, killing version of Norma Bates, still possessing Norma's biting wit and sense of humor, but absolutely none of Norma's charm or sweetness and over the course of the series, Norma Bates did lighten up and become sweeter. #2 is could Norman carry the series the way Norma did? Hell, yes! The young phenom Freddie Highmore not only completely carried the series as Norman Bates, he stole the show and took it to new, unforeseen heights that I didn't think possible. Now the central and sole main character, Norman got to interact with every other major character and so he was the common thread that held the storylines to Season 5 together. And Highmore was utterly brilliant from start to finish. Interestingly, this trajectory of the series is somewhat like the film where one character was the star of the first act, then another took over in the second half. This is what it was like on Bates Motel where Norma led the way the first 3 seasons, then Norman kind of took over in the last 2 seasons. As much as I thought Highmore deserved an Emmy nomination for Season 4 (he didn't get one), he should totally get one for Season 5, and dare I say if he does, his name should be the one called when the envelope is opened on Emmy night! Highmore's Norman is way deeper and more complex than even the legendary version created onscreen by Anthony Perkins in the classic 1960 film of which this series borrowed heavily from. Being a long-running show, it was able to illustrate how and why Norman became who he ended up from a firsthand account. We've seen his psychosis evolve since the Pilot, culminating into his pure descent into madness in Season 5. #3 was the very dubious casting of none other than pop music sensation Rihanna as the iconic Marion Crane character! And I wasn't alone in disliking this decision as many fans were calling BS on this odd casting choice. Rihanna's certainly not an accomplished actress by any stretch (in fact having received the very dishonorable Razzie for her "performance" in the awful film Battleship) and the acting on this series, even from actors playing minor characters, has been pretty rock solid over the years. So I was NOT looking forward to watching Rihanna attempt to blend in with this world created by showrunners Carlton Cuse and Keri Ehrin. In all honesty, overall Rihanna was actually OK in the part and really didn't ruin anything. Could she have been better? Yes, but in fact especially in the scenes where she acted off of Highmore, thankfully, the experienced beyond his years young actor really helped her performance along and even somewhat keep pace with him in their scenes. In fact, I dare say the show's re-creation of the iconic Norman-Marion parlor scene is close to up there with it's 1960 predecessor. So it all worked out in the end. The plot of Season 5 starts about a year and a half after the Season 4 finale. With Norma dead, Norman now runs the motel full time and in the process befriends a newcomer to White Pine Bay in the form of Madeline Loomis (extremely well played by gifted newcomer Isabelle McNally). Madeline is essentially a 10 years younger version of Norma, looking a lot like her and thus why Norman takes an interest in her. Madeline runs the local hardware store and forms a business arrangement with Norman to supply the motel with needed amenities. Things get complicated as Norman and Madeline form a strong bond. Similar to Norman, Madeline is a very lonely woman whose husband Sam Loomis (solidly played by Austin Nichols) is a travelling businessman who spends a lot of time in Seattle. Madeline and Norman's mutual attraction is the genesis of some major plot points later in the season and culminates in several tragic occurrences. Meanwhile, Norman's brother Dylan Massett (superbly played by Max Thierot) and his now-wife Emma DeCody (excellently played by Olivia Cooke) are happily married with a daughter living in Seattle away from the craziness of the Bates' family back home. Dylan hasn't made contact with Norman since the falling out he had with both him and Norma in late Season 4, so he's unaware of Norma's death. Also returning for the final season is Alex Romero (stolidly played by the reliable Nestor Carbonell), who is serving a prison sentence after having been arrested in the Season 4 finale for obstruction of justice in the crimes he was party to in town while he was the sheriff. Speaking of, the new town lawperson is Sheriff Jane Greene (strongly played by Brooke Smith), who in her own way is as no-nonsense and insightful as Romero was, except she is strictly by the book. Also returning is Norma's brother Caleb Calhoun (again well played by Kenny Johnson), who wants to make amends with Dylan and Norma up on his return to the states from self-imposed exile in Mexico. And last by certainly not least and probably my favorite supporting character not only in Season 5 but also the entire series there is Chick Hogan (wonderfully essayed by Ryan Hurst), the extremely quirky, morbid, macabre Mountain Man type character first introduced back in Season 3. Chick develops a weird, yet fascinating relationship with Norman in Season 5 after meeting him in the Season 4 finale. Their scenes are among my favorite of the entire season. Every episode in Season 5 felt like a sheer masterpiece. Not a single wasted moment or scene. And much more so than earlier seasons which were more combination of melodrama and suspense, Season 5 felt like pure full-on horror! Very much akin to the final act of Psycho itself. By the end of it all, the series created not only one but TWO iconic TV characters that will forever light up screens upon re-watch, Norma Bates and NORMAN BATES! Well done, Cuse and Ehrin. Very well done!

After 2 great seasons of this series THE FLASH, it finally hit a wall in Season 3! Where do I begin? Let me count the ways: I frankly saw this coming but I knew that Barry Allen and Iris West were not right for each other on this series. I'm not a canon aficionado, but in Season 1 (especially) and Season 2, I was just not feeling this supposedly epic love story of WestAllen (the ship name for Barry and Iris). In Season 1, Barry unhealthily stalked Iris while she was with the sweet, genuine nice guy Eddie Thawne, while Iris played around with both their feelings and resonated as a manipulative bitch much of the way. I was in the group that did not sign on for Barry and Iris ever becoming a thing on this show, even though we all knew it had to happen at some point. But I was just glad it hadn't happened yet. In Season 2, they brought in Patty Spivot for Barry and while that wasn't a great relationship, Barry sure as hell seemed a lot HAPPIER in her orbit than he ever has in Iris'. So Barry and Patty broke up over some contrived BS because he wouldn't tell her he's the Flash, then that opened the door for Iris to get over Eddie's demise from Season 1, then snake her way into Barry's personal space and inner circle late into Season 2. But Barry thankfully wasn't ready as he was dealing with his father Henry's death. This leads us to Season 3. Barry has created this alternate reality called Flashpoint where both his parents are alive and well into his adulthood, but his compadres from the main timeline Joe, Iris, Wally, Cisco, and Caitlin, don't know who he is. After a bad encounter with the metahuman Rival, who mortally wounds Wally, who is known as Kid Flash in this alternate reality, Barry tries to re-form the Team Flash to save him, but can't. So he decides, with Reverse Flash's help, who he was keeping prisoner after stopping him from killing his Mom in the Season 2 finale, Barry allows his speedster rival to go through with his Mom's murder so the show's main timeline can be restored, but something goes wrong. Things change when Barry gets back to the timeline: Joe and Iris aren't on speaking terms, Cisco's brother has died in a car accident, and Caitlin now has cold powers from the particle accelerator explosion that occurred back in Season 1. And Barry can't fix it! So now everyone has to continue on in this alternate timeline. This is where the show screwed up. Flashpoint lasted for ONE episode! Barry screws up everyone's life over an impulsive decision in the Season 2 finale. Everyone's live are messed up somehow, but by some miracle, Barry and Iris are a couple! This is even after erasing their Season 2 finale kiss. This was the part I wish weren't true because them as a couple singlehandedly ruined Season 3. I don't think I've ever seen such an incredibly sugary, corny relationship with such juvenile drivel dialogue in my life, and that's saying something with all the angsty melodramatic love stories out there. The writers pulled out every possible cliché from the books for these 2. It's like watching a high school play. They don't interact like 2 adults, but like 2 lovesick teens. I might have believed this if not for the fact that Iris decided to be with Barry SOLELY because of the destiny thing. She literally said this was the reason she wanted a relationship with Barry back in late Season 2. We're married in the future and on Earth-2, so let's go for it! All of a sudden in Season 3, because of this couple, the show became about their passionless, chemistry-lacking romance and everyone had to fawn over them and bow to their feet. The writers literally created a subplot, the Savitar prophecy that started in the mid-season finale, where Barry accidentally went to the future and saw the evil speedster Savitar kill Iris before his very eyes, to try and make Iris West relevant on this series. And during this entire subplot that lasted for all of the second half of the season, Iris still had absolutely no good writing or development, just like in the first 2 seasons. Instead, it was all focused on Barry and how her pending doom affected him and Joe, but not Iris herself. So the writers basically expected fans to care about a confusing, soulless, boring character such as Iris West just because we have to? Barry and Joe love her, we love Barry and Joe, so we've got to root for Iris to live to continue to be an irrelevant, dull character for future seasons? Essentially, an entire season was wasted. While he was in this romance with Iris and due to the Savitar prophecy and Flashpoint, Barry became less heroic, started ignoring his friends' fates and had to be kicked in the rear at times to even go out and fight crime. His attitude was basically all this saving people and helping my friends can be put on hold until I figure out a way to save Iris first. Iris spent the bulk of Season 3 telling Barry not to lose himself, but that's exactly what he did because of his involvement with HER. Grant Gustin continued to excel as Barry but his character become too damn moody and sullen in Season 3 and rather dickish at times. I missed the more fun, lighthearted, positive-outlook, heart-of-gold Barry from the first 2 seasons. Caitlin's Killer Frost storyline was the salvation of Season 3 with Danielle Panabaker stepping up to the plate as the standout and her episode 3x07 titled "Killer Frost" as the best of the season. Another plus was the addition of Tom Felton (from Harry Potter fame) as Julian Albert, a fellow CSI and metahuman expert and foil for Barry. Felton really grew up since his Harry Potter days and developed into a good actor. I usually love Tom Cavanagh, but didn't really care for the new Season 3 version Wells they went with, HR. I think he was overly comical and too high-strung. I kept wanting him to dial it down a notch more often than not. Jesse L Martin continued to shine as Joe West, but he wasn't given much to do except worry about Iris and pull out his gun, that and get his own disposable love interest. Carlos Valdez also acquitted himself well as Cisco, but like Barry, Cisco turned into a sourpuss for much of the season. I'm just going to say it, Candace Patton is terrible as Iris West! Her bad acting and bludgeoning of dialogue stands out like a sore thumb on this show. She makes Iris into this melodramatic, awkward character who just doesn't fit in with the tone of this series. I ignored it mostly in Seasons 1 and 2 when she was back burner, but in Season 3 with her in a lot more scenes because of the love story and always being in the team StarLabs scenes, it's painfully noticeable she has no range in her acting, at least not on this show. She's a one-trick pony, her role always to be emotional about everything and look sad all the time, and when she looks happy, it never feels genuine, like she's going through the motions. I've always gotten the sense that Iris' character on this show has an air of superiority, as if she's above all the silliness and nonsense. While all the other actors seem to know what type of series they are in and they all know how to be funny. Iris is humorless and it always feels like she's on another show from everyone else. In Season 3, there were so many filler episodes where nothing seemed to happen. Barry whines and worries about Iris or rants at someone. Yet he screwed up more than anyone the whole season. Characters keeping secrets from the team. Nothing coming of it. A big thing will happen one episode then get resolved the next and swept under the rug like it didn't happen. No flow to the storytelling at all. Episodes feeling disjointed from each other. The season big bad villain Savitar acting intimidating but ultimately boring. Reverse Flash and Zoom were much better villains in Seasons 1 and 2, respectively. An overabundance of characters with superpowers: Barry, Cisco, Wally, Caitlin, Jesse, yet very little gets accomplished. Barry did more in Season 1 acting alone than in Season 3 when multiple characters would go out into the field. Team Flash getting too big. Characters like Iris and HR being there and being utterly useless. The absolute worst episodes were the 2-part Grodd arc (completely underwhelming and a waste of time) and a freakin MUSICAL episode! A schmaltz, filler of an episode where there was ironically barely any singing, the "plot" was stupid, and the end of which is the single most cringe moment in the history of TV. Makes me wonder where the extra star is coming from! The only reason I give the extra star is due to consistent acting from MOST of the cast and the Killer Frost subplot. Otherwise, a sad junior season to this initially promising series.

People REALLY need to take off their rose-colored glasses when it comes to this movie! TOMBSTONE (1993) is about one of the most cringy, cheesy big summer movies that has come out of Hollywood, and that's saying something. Now, I'm not a prude when it comes to film. I understand that most movies are meant to entertain. They don't have to always inform, be so serious, or teach the viewer a lesson. I've seen my share of non-serious movies in my day, but Tombstone is one of those movies that feels like it's supposed to have an air of seriousness underneath all of the bloat and bluster. It's not supposed to be a silly, throwaway summer movie, but that is EXACTLY what it comes across as. It is a mirage of being something more than it truly is. For some unearthly reason, people seem to love this movie, but I find it unintentionally funny in a lot of places. For one, there are way too many characters in this movie, at least half of them useless and nary leaving an impression. It feels like the casting director just decided to populate it with a bunch of B-to-C list actors hoping the total would amount to more than the sum of the parts. Not one single character in this movie "spoke to me". And even in the most throwaway movies, I expect to have characters that I can relate to, like, or at the very least understand. Kurt Russell dubiously stars in the main role of Wyatt Earp and much as I like most of Russell's work, this is easily one of his most bland film performances. Russell seems like such a fake tough guy throughout this movie, acting like a big bully when most of the guys he tangled with looked like they could easily kick his ass! He wasn't intimidating in the slightest. And as the star, I felt no emotions towards his character's success or failure. He was just incredibly 1-dimensional. Now, to the most lauded performance of the movie, Val Kilmer as Doc Holiday. Of all the performances in the movie, I suppose that Kilmer is the standout and I've certainly never seen him play any other role in this manner, but I found his character too much comedy which served as an odd counterbalance to everything else, which was supposedly more serious. Every other word out of Holiday's mouth was some kind of joke or insult to the character he was speaking to. Even in the most tense action scenes, he was making light of everything. And I didn't think Russell and Kilmer had any semblance of onscreen buddy chemistry. To the supporting cast, which included that aforementioned group of B-to-C list actors (maybe even a couple of Ds thrown in for good measure): Sam Elliott, Bill Paxton, Powers Boothe, Michael Biehn, Dana Delany, Stephen Lang, Thomas Haden Church, Jason Priestley, Billy Zane, Billy Bob Thornton, and none other than Charlton Heston (see what I mean about the big cast?), absolutely NONE of these actors left any kind of an impression in their moments in the movie. They ranged from overly silly and obnoxious (like Lang as Ike Clanton and Zane as the effeminate actor) to downright awful (like Paxton as Morgan Earp and Priestley as the town joke). In between, it was just sheer blandness! In addition, Delany was utterly unsexy and silly as the supposedly hot actress Josephine that served as Wyatt's love interest. She and Russell had zero chemistry and their romance felt incredibly forced. What's really weird is that Delany has looked way hotter in most other things I've seen her in, so why, when she's playing man-loving vixen, would they make her look so drab? Tombstone feels as a series of loud, blustery vignettes, which every scene of actors trying to outshine each other with actors unnecessarily shouting their dialogue at each other. Then for some reason, after about close to 2 hours of silliness and bluster, the movie goes all sentimental and mushy. Just end the movie the way you presented it, as a bunch of filler silliness! The movie was directed by George P. Cosmatos. and I'm not surprised I've never heard of this director before or since this movie!

It's really no contest for me, but WEIRD SCIENCE (1985) is my favorite John Hughes movie! Is it the best? Debatable, but it is EASILY his most hilariously funny, entertaining, most fun movie start to finish. There is no let up, no slow parts, no wasted moments. Just humorous from the hilarious opening to the equally hilarious closing sequence, in which the film goes full circle. The absurd premise of the movie is that 2 barely pubescent horny teenagers 15-year olds Gary (a brilliant Anthony-Michael Hall) and Wyatt (newcomer Ilan-Mitchell Smith), bored on a Friday night while Wyatt's parents are away for the weekend, decide to create a beautiful woman for themselves after watching The Bride of Frankenstein on TV. Using Wyatt's computer, with a little hacking, an Operation Game, a fashion magazine, and a couple of head bras thrown in for good measure (LOL), the nerd duo indeed create a woman, in the form of Lisa (superbly played by 80s babe Kelly McGillis), a tall, slender, voluptuous, savvy, sexy model. The movie also features Chet (winningly played by Bill Paxton), who is Wyatt's boorish older brother visiting while on leave from the military. The comic performances from these actors, in particular Hall (who really owns the movie), McGillis (surprisingly hilarious) and Paxton (who specializes in playing funny a-holes) are completely memorable and are just as funny today as they were 30 years ago. Smith is most obviously the least experienced of the group, but he acquits himself very well and thankfully is carried by the more seasoned trio of Hall, McGillis, and Paxton. Smith kind of breaks the 4th wall and smiles a LOT throughout the movie, but it strangely kind of works given how utterly ridiculous the premise is. Weird Science also features several funny small roles, in particular a couple of wannabe bullies in Ian (played by the now famous Robert Downey Jr) and Max (Robert Rusler, what happened to this guy?) who terrorize Gary and Wyatt at points throughout the movie, their girlfriends Deb and Hilly (Suzanne Snyder and Judie Aronson) who both Gary and Wyatt have crushes on, an aging punk rock biker gang leader (wonderfully played by reliable 80s bad guy Vernon Wells), and Dino (played by John Hughes' stalwart John Kapelos, who also was in 'The Breakfast Club' with Hall), part of the group of blues brothers who hung out at the bar that Lisa takes the boys too, where Hall steals the show with a drunk Gary acting out singing the blues. There are just so many funny scenes and iconic moments in this movie. Some highlights: the opening gym scene, the blues club sequence, the boys first confrontation with Chet, the meeting between Lisa and Gary's parents (my absolute favorite scene of the film), the boys' bathroom scenes at the party, the second creation sequence at the party which results in the funny montage of Wyatt's home getting wrecked (piano girl part is a hoot), the kitchen confrontation between Lisa and Chet where she puts him in his place in a very interesting way. In particular, Hall delivers a genius comic performance as Gary, replete with funny facial expressions, great physical comedy, perfect line delivery, as well as tons of charm. It's one of my all time favorite lead comic performances in ANY film! And as previously stated, McGillis performance is also on the money, managing to make Lisa simultaneously sexy, sweet, seductive, charming, lethal, controlling, and funny. She has more range in this movie than most actresses do in much more lauded films, both comic and otherwise. The scene where she squares off with Gary's stern father, as I mentioned before, makes me laugh my rear end off every time I see it. And as I said before, Smith's contribution should not go unnoticed, especially since he's featured in a lot of scenes. He has several funny moments and it really helps playing off of Hall and his antics for most of the movie. Hughes must have had a ball making this piece. It's easily the most convoluted of his movies, arguably the only one not really grounded in any kind of plot realism or bogged down with overly serious moments. Yeah, there's the awkward, nerdy teen thing and 80s vibe, but this movie truly stands the test of time and is a true comic masterpiece as far as I'm concerned. A lot of people would probably qualify this as a silly, toilet humor, dumb comedy, but that's completely wrong, in my opinion. The humor in this movie is genuinely amenable to many people's tastes and I find a lot of the dialogue well-written. It's not a disgusting, cringy comic piece like a lot of so-called "laugh out loud" comedies that Hollywood churns out in today's film. Weird Science is just plain funny and does what a film comedy is supposed to do, make people laugh.

I guess because I loved this series so much back in it's freshman season (still the best season, which pretty much explains it all in terms of later seasons), I kept sticking with it for some unearthly reason. Maybe it was because I grew up watching at a time when virtually EVERY series did at least 20 episodes per season and I'm nostalgic. Limited episode series (10, 11, or 12) take so long to come back, at least 22 to 23 seasonal episodic shows I don't have to wait as long for them to get back to business. So every season, with ONCE UPON A TIME, I just keep coming back, hoping for who knows what! Well, I can easily say that the MAIN reason I started do dislike this series has to do with that character on the cover for Season 5! None other than Killian Jones, AKA Captain Hook, one of the worst main characters I've ever seen on a long-running popular series. I don't care that this crap excuse of a character has so many fans or that showrunners continue to force his face and the Captain Swan ship onto the audience, Hook is, has always been, and will always be, a terrible character! He was a poor excuse for a villain (on a show where they are usually the best characters!) and he's an equally poor excuse for a hero. He's just a pretty boy that a bunch of teen girls fawned over and threatened to quit the show if he didn't end up with Emma instead of the more deep, promising character of Neal, who they didn't find nearly as physically appealing. It's a sad, painful truth, but it IS the truth! Season 2 introduced the wretched Hook character and spent the bulk of his time twirling his mustache and hitting on everything in sight, then the writers proceeded to have him stalk and sleazebag his way into Emma's life in Season 3. Season 4 the writers called themselves taking it slow with Captain Swan and turning Hook into some kind of low-rent hero, regardless of all the immoral, evil things he'd done already. In fairness, this series specializes in turning most of it's villains into heroes. It became the thing to do once they redeemed Regina, it's first villain. They just said, screw it, everyone gets to be redeemed! Season 5, the one I'm reviewing, unfortunately spends a fair amount of time continuing to try and ingratiate the sickening Captain Swan romance onto the viewer, with Emma Swan (the main character and only one with any kind of meaty material anymore; got to give credit to Jennifer Morrison for being somewhat interesting as the Dark One) going all Dark One and dragging her so-called true love Hook's sorry tail with her. The show spent half a season with this nonsense, then Hook sacrifices himself (yadda yadda) and of course instead of opting to be grateful that she still has her REAL family, Henry and the Charmings, she instead opts to drag everyone to the Underworld to save Captain Loser! But before that, it involved all the heroes travelling to Camelot to find a way to keep Emma from giving into her newfound darkness. The Camelot subplot was terrible, with the writers turning Arthur into a major douche and wasting time on knighthood, balls, and Henry's puberty finally kicking in! Actually, it was the Underworld story in the second half of Season 5 as to why I'm giving it the extra 2 stars because I found that subplot surprisingly enjoyable. Why? Well, for one the writers smartly kept the Captain Swan drivel to a bare minimum. Even though the mission was to save Hook, it ended up playing last fiddle to several more interesting storylines. For one, there was the introduction of Hades (played to the hilt by gifted comic actor Greg Germann), a mercurial combination of humor mixed with deadly seriousness. Secondly, there was a very interesting subplot involving Hades and Rumple (the always reliable Robert Carlyle). Third, there were some nice subplots involving characters getting to reunite and make amends with their departed loved ones, like Emma and Neal (who is her real true love as far as I'm concerned), Regina and HenrySr, Regina and Daniel, Zelena and Cora, Belle and Gaston, David and James, and Rumple and Pan. All these subplots were beautifully handled by the writers and paid great tribute to the show's history. But last and not least was the character progression and development of Zelena (beautifully acted by Rebecca Mader). Zelena had true epiphany in Season 5 with the birth of her baby and realizing she had to be better for her child. Mader's performance was filled with subtlety and depth. Also, I loved the romance between Zelena and Hades! Really the first ship in a while that I really rooted for, despite it involved 2 villainous characters. Mader and Germann had tremendous chemistry. Interestingly, Season 5 was the first season where I thought the B part was not only better than the A part, but far exceeded it. In both Seasons 3 and 4, the A part was much better than B, but a lot of it was simply by default as the B half-seasons were sheer boredom. It's no surprise that simply by not focusing on Captain Swan once they got to the B-plot in the Underworld, the show improved greatly for part A! Unfortunately, the writers have continued to pimp this trash relationship into Season 6, which I've already seen. It's just so sad that this once very promising series allowed itself to get hijacked by such an ill-conceived, soulless romance that is Captain Swan!

SABAN'S POWER RANGERS (2017) easily has to be biggest, most pleasant movie surprise of the summer of 2017! I had ZERO intention of even watching this thing, ended up almost accidentally deciding to give it a go bored one Saturday evening, the early scene consisting of 2 high school ne'er do wells kidnapping a cow as part of a school prank (yeah, right) and thought, well, I'm not going to make it past 15 minutes of this thing before turning it off. THEN, immediately, a surprisingly thought-provoking scene between father and son, one of the aforementioned high school pranksters, about responsibility, maturity, and thinking about his future. I slowly got sucked in. The son is high school football star Jason Scott (played with great conviction and excellence by newcomer Dacre Montgomery), who is thrown in Saturday detention for his misdeed. There he meets fellow troubled youths cheerleader Kimberly Hart (wonderfully played by newcomer Naomi Scott) and autistic science geek Billy Cranston (brilliantly performed in scene-stealing fashion by newcomer RJ Cyler). The 3 youths cross paths at the local town mine and meet 2 other of their fellow high-schoolers, the rebellious loner Trini (winningly played by newcomer Becky G) and the thrill-seeking hothead Zack (well played by newcomer Ludi Lin). Jason=Red Ranger, Kim=Purple Ranger, Billy=Blue Ranger, Trini=Yellow Ranger, Zack=Black Ranger. I had never heard of any of this group of actors before and was mightily impressed with their casting, acting, and chemistry. The 5 teens are "chosen" to defeat the evil Rita Repulsa (played to the hilt by gifted comic actress, the veteran Elizabeth Backs) by Zordon (the previous Red Ranger, voiced well by "Mr. Breaking Bad" himself Bryan Cranston) and his cute little wisecracking robot sidekick Alpha 5 (voiced by the hilarious chameleon Bill Hader). The mine serves as the team's base of operations where they alternate between training and arguing until they finally come together not as newly superpowered beings, but as a group of connected teens who relate to each other's real-world problems. The humor works incredibly throughout, even veering into witty territory at times. The lighthearted tone was always underneath the surface of the, dare I say it, powerful drama. And as mentioned before, the acting was incredibly strong across the group of gifted young newbies. Expecting this romp to be nothing more than a throwaway, silly, cheesy, summer kids movie, I was stunned at how it managed to avoid clichés and really be ABOUT something! To my surprise, the movie actually built up the character relationships for the first 2/3 of the movie, really forming convincing bonds among the 5 troubled youths. The last 1/3 of course is mostly action, but thanks to the buildup, I actually gave a damn about the survival of this unit of teens. I am honestly looking forward to the sequel!

history.title: Alien: Covenant
history.review_title: Underrated and a strong addition to the Alien brand
history.text: ALIEN:COVENANT (2017) had the deck stacked against it going in. It had the arduous task of both trying to live up to Ridley Scott's more revered '79 Alien masterpiece as well as James Cameron's widely acclaimed action sequel, '86 Aliens, PLUS it had to both somewhat make up for Scott's dubious '12 prequel Prometheus with it's mixed reaction. Prometheus was a movie that was hyped to the hilt and made a ton of money, but alternated between being hailed some ethereal "people just don't get it" masterpiece (a la 2001) versus a pretentious, bloated, flashy, terribly acted CGI exercise that was nothing more than hot garbage. Count me in the latter group! LOL I really dislike Prometheus and can't get past it's utterly stupid characterizations which sank the film for me. At the end of the day, I think character trumps CGI, something I randomly preach in my reviews. I'll take character over effects any day of the week and twice on Sunday. For myself, in terms of characters, Alien:Covenant absolutely craps on Prometheus for the simple fact that not a single character in Covenant ANNOYED me, while virtually every single character in Prometheus accomplished that dubious feat! To me, Covenant is the 2nd best Alien film (minority opinion, I know) and it's not really saying much as Scott's '79 film Alien is one of the great multi-genre (sci-fi, horror, thriller, character study) of all time. The overrated '86 sequel Aliens is just an abrasive summer action flick, nothing more. Then there's the underwhelming Alien3 and Alien:Resurrection. And of course the massive disappointment Prometheus. So Covenant didn't have much to overcome. What Covenant did that Prometheus failed to do is keep it simple: simple story, simple characters, simple plot and in doing so, culminates in a very re-watchable, enjoyable summer movie experience. Also, unlike Prometheus, Covenant actually makes me look forward to the next sequel! Covenant starts with a prologue sequence of the creation of the android David (the best character from Prometheus, reprised by the great Michael Fassbender) in the early 21st century by billionaire Peter Weyland (well played in esteemed fashion by Guy Pearce, also reprising his role, but this time as the young version of Weyland). Peter and David converse about the human condition and the irony that even though Weyland created him, David will actually live forever while Weyland is destined to expire, like all humans. Flash forward to the early 22nd century and the colonial spaceship Covenant, maintained on it's way to the habitable Origae-6 planetary system by the ship's synthetic being Walter (also played by Fassbender in a completely believable dual role). The ship encounters a solar flare which causes it's life-support systems to malfunction, compelling Walter to get the ship's main computer "Mother" to awake the 14-member crew from cryosleep and fix the ship, which is also carrying 2000 colonists still in cryosleep and over 1000 embryos for building a new world. With the incident causing the original Captain's cryotube to fail and burn up, the leadership role is taken over by Captain Oram (excellently played by veteran actor Billy Crudup). Oram is a man of faith and a bit shaken by the incident and unsure of if the crew trusts his leadership style. The 2nd-in-command is the feisty Daniels (strongly played by Katherine Waterston), the wife of the original captain who must soldier on without her husband. Rounding out the main characters are down-to-earth ship's pilot Tennessee (winningly played by Danny McBride), stalwart crew biologist and Oram's wife Karine (stolidly played by Carmen Ejogo), crew shuttle pilot and Tennessee's wife Faris (confidently played by Amy Seimetz), security team leader Sergeant Lope (cheekily played by Demian Bichir), and married crew co-pilots Upworth and Ricks (solidly played by Callie Hernandez and Jussie Smollett). Upon repairing the ship, the crew discovers a transmission on a nearby (and apparently life-sustaining) planet and go to investigate the distress signal as well as research and map out the planet as a permanent home in lieu of traveling for another 7 years to Origae-6. Upon touching down, the planet at first appears perfect, but as the group further investigates, it's not long before things turn out to good to be true, and the group runs into trouble and must navigate their way out of it somehow. Surprisingly, the film has a healthy amount of action and the scenes are all tense and edge-of-your-seat. The aliens are pretty intimidating and agile in this as Covenant combines elements from the 3 most popular films of the franchise Alien, Aliens, and Prometheus. Yet I feel as if Covenant stands well on it's own as an entertaining horror-thriller-action movie. I feel as if Covenant took the "less is more" approach and succeeded in spades! I had to re-watch Covenant (glad to do it) to realize how perfectly modulated the supporting performances were and how in sync the actors played off each other to resonate as a real crew. Just subtle things showed these people had known each other for a long time and I liked the way their rather by-the-numbers dialogue bounced off each other very naturally. While Fassbender easily stole the show as Walter/David (doesn't he always?), the rest of the actors should be commended for being very natural in their performances, unlike the characters in Prometheus who felt like cardboard cutout cartoons most of the time. I think the people roasting this movie for bad performances and weak, stupid characters do it a major disservice. I think they are conflating it too much with Prometheus, which is an abomination in terms of both character and acting. The characters in Covenant behaved very real to me, the way they reacted to the rather crazy circumstances they encountered. The shocks, the jump scares, the reactions all felt genuine. I might say that I tend to agree that the CGI wasn't the greatest, but as I've repeatedly said, I'll take character over CGI anyday and for me, the characters worked in this film, along with many other elements that kept it entertaining from start to finish. I would say this movie is underrated and give it a few years and people will re-visit Covenant as the deserving addition to the Alien franchise it truly is.

I'm a person who generally leans toward the original films of a franchise more so than the sequel, but there are exceptions, in particular in this case. INDIANA JONES AND THE TEMPLE OF DOOM (1984) is the best film of the franchise to me. It's the one I watch on repeat repeatedly. Fast-paced, chock full of action, humor, wit, charm, and heart, not only is it my favorite Indy film, it's one of my favorite Steven Spielberg films. And what's alarming to me is how many people don't even rank this as the 2nd best Indy flick! I think a lot of fans actually believe that the 1989 film 'The Last Crusade', an overrated, cheesy-looking, dated, humorless, pretentious, poorly acted, boring exercise and test on my patience, is the 2nd best film, or dare I even say it, the best one! That flick is nothing more than a re-hash of the original film 'Raiders of the Lost Ark', replete with Nazis and world-changing biblical artifact. Actually a prequel to 'Raiders', 'Temple of Doom' is set in 1935 and starts off with a slam bang musical number 'Anything Goes' in a fancy Hong Kong nightclub where our hero Dr. Indiana Jones (excellently played by film icon Harrison Ford in probably my all-time favorite performance of his) squares off against a prominent Chinese gangster over a precious diamond and as chaos ensues in a wild action sequence of the club patrons barreling out of the nightclub, Indy makes his escape along with Willie Scott (wonderfully played in scene-stealing fashion by Kate Capshaw), an American entertainer who sang the opening number. Along with Willie, accompanying Indy is his sidekick Short Round (funny performance by then child actor Jonathan Ke Quan). I'll never understand how people thought Willie and Short Round were annoying in this flick, when Capshaw and Quan displayed wonderful comic timing and actually had believable chemistry with Harrison Ford. It was like following the adventures of a fractured family and this trio as the heart of the film really makes it work, all their interactions feeling natural and heartwarming. I honestly thought Ford had a more believable family bond with Short Round than with Sean Connery as his Dad in 'Crusade', which I thought reeked of Hollywood one-liners. After a narrow escape from their abandoned plane on a life raft, they fall into a wild river in India and make their way to a village where the leader indicates all of the local children have been kidnapped by a malevolent occult leader Mola Ram (Amrish Puri in a vigorous, wide-eyed, scary performance), who is holed up at the luxurious Pangkot Palace. The trio makes their way to the palace and get into the thick of things immediately as Indy investigates and finds that the palace royalty is in cahoots with the cult leader and finds Mola Ram's base of operations in the cavernous structures beneath the palace. The adventure ensues as Indy tries to stop Mola Ram and save the children from being cult sacrifices. A huge reason that 'Temple of Doom' stands out for me over all other Indy films is that there is no let up. The movie starts out with that entertaining musical number, moves straight into the action and never lets go. The dialogue is crisp, the humor still fresh, the action scenes still hold up due to very limited, if any, CGI, and the performances are energetic. 'Raiders' has always felt like a bunch of nicely staged set pieces to me that add up to an entertaining film, while 'Crusade' is just awful. But 'Temple' feels right, the most fluid of all the Indy flicks with the best ending. Spielberg does a great job of balancing several elements: action, horror, the occult, romance, family drama, and meshes all these into a film that will forever be entertaining.

history.review_title: Overlong, boring, and not enough Michael Keaton!
history.text: SPIDER-MAN HOMECOMING (2017) was the most anticipated movie of the summer. I was planning to go see it in theatres, but never got around to it and so glad I didn't! The only part I wish I was there for was that hilarious ending. I'm not lying when I say that the ending was damn near the ONLY funny part of the movie. Clocking in at well over 2 hours, after the 1st hour, I badly wanted this movie to be over. This is one of the slowest, most boring superhero movies I've ever seen. And it was supposed to be funny and I think I laughed maybe only 3 or 4 times throughout. Full disclosure, I've never watched any of the Avenger movies and really don't care about them. I only care about Batman, Superman, Spider-Man, and Wonder Woman. And speaking of great superhero movies, this year's Wonder Woman was so much BETTER than Spider-Man Homecoming (SMH for short, perfect initials). SMH stars teen actor Tom Holland (never seen him in anything before) as the titular character Spider-Man aka Peter Parker. Holland does a great job masking his British accent, I found to be very uncharismatic and annoying in this role. I swear, the first 90 minutes of the movie, this kid wouldn't shut up! Lol The dude talked and talked and talked, and he talked TO HIMSELF more than he did other people. Even when he was alone, he was making annoying sidecracking remarks and I literally shouted at the screen for him to shut it (he had me talking to myself!). Faring much better and making Peter somewhat tolerable is his best friend and fellow classmate Ned (well played by Jacob Batalon), whose jokes actually DID work. And it was really only the scenes with Ned (and another character I'll mention later) that I even cared about Peter with. Ned may have been the cliché, comic relief sidekick, but at least he did his job and made me laugh more often than not. Now, the other teen characters didn't fare so well. Peter's other primary classmates, who were all on the academic team with him and Ned, are Flash (Peter's rival played by Tony Revolori), Michelle (cliché wisecracking goth girl), and Liz (Peter's love interest). Flash is no longer a scary, athletic, intimidating bully, but a puny loser that even the slight and nerdy Peter could take out WITHOUT his powers. Michelle was such a cliché, the loner rebel, unattractive girl and her lines were delivered in such a bland and annoying manner by the actress. Liz is the cliché beautiful love interest and I swear the actress looks like she's pushing 30 playing a 15-year old? And overall the adult characters didn't fare much better with the sole exception of the great Michael Keaton, who played Peter's rival Adrian Toomes AKA Vulture. Keaton can do roles like this in his sleep. Similar to how he gave the best performance in the otherwise tedious Robocop reboot, Keaton steals the show in SMH with a performance full of controlled menace. I did like the hero-villain confrontations between Spidey and Vulture. Marisa Tomei was so-so as Peter's Aunt May, but the script did her no favors. And I don't know why people complained about Aunt May being a hot cougar. Peter is 15 damn years old. His aunt could easily have been played by someone in their 30s, even late 20s! It's not crazy for a teenager to have a youngish aunt. And Robert Downey Jr (as Tony Stark) and Jon Favreau (as his assistant Happy Hogan, that truly his real name?) were just there. Were these 2 characters supposed to be funny? Like I said, I don't watch Avenger movies, so I don't know the beat of these characters, but it shouldn't matter since they are part of a movie that belongs to Spider-Man. The plot of this tedious exercise is that teen Parker, who has his powers at the start of the movie already has just come back from a summer "internship" with Stark Enterprises. I remember seeing a youtube clip of Stark, Peter, and May at the end of one of those Avenger movie that I refuse to watch, so I guess Peter got his powers in that earlier film. The early part of the movie is a 10-minute student film of Peter and his experiences in Berlin with Stark (Iron Man) and the other Avengers, including Captain America and the Hulk. That's as far as I got with the character names, the rest I just don't know. Peter is a chatty teen who annoys the hell out of Stark and Happy (really?) about joining the Avengers full time. The 2 men ignore Peter much of the film and leave him to his own devices as Stark tells Peter to just enjoy life and be a high-school student and a "friendly neighborhood" Spider-Man, which is exactly what Peter does for about the first 30 minutes of the movie. Meanwhile, in another part of the city, Adrian Toomes (excellently played by Keaton), a former city salvage worker who confiscated a bunch of alien artifacts 8 years earlier in the film's prologue, is running an illegal parts-selling operation to the city's low-level criminals. Toomes and his crew (including Logan Marshall green and Bookeem Woodbine, both actors pretty lifeless in their roles, as the 2 Shockers) have morphed the artifacts into powerful weapons, including the creation of a Vulture weapon, operated by Toomes himself, an enormous flying alien craft molded into the form of a vulture. These effects were pretty cool. So Peter stumbles onto the operation accidentally and then neglects his normal responsibilities, which includes skipping school and dumping his academic team duties. The movie has 2 climaxes, one at the halfway mark at the Washington monument, which was actually a tense scene with too much humor and the final confrontation between Spider-Man and Vulture, which is was pretty invigorating and edge-of-your-seat. But unfortunately the humor just didn't work for the most part. Keaton fared the best in his role because his character wasn't hampered by cheesy, stupid dialogue like most of the other characters. He got to play a more grounded, real character with genuine dialogue and you could feel his menace emanate through his performance. Holland should probably be cut some slack since he is a literal teen in real life and had to carry a major summer movie, but if you're going to play with the big boys, then you've got to take the criticism along with the praises.

Season 3 of FTWD really stepped up it's game, and this is in light of a MAJOR character death early in the season! In just 3x02, the showrunners had the gumption to kill off fan favorite Travis (brilliantly portrayed by the great Cliff Curtis), due to the actor obligation to a pending major film project. I was sure the show would go down the drain once he died because Travis was my absolute favorite character. And with Travis' ex-wife Liza (killed in Season 1 finale) and son Chris (killed in Season 2 finale), that meant no more Manawas, who I loved way more than the Clarks. Thankfully, the show managed to over compensate for the very underwhelming Clark family Madison (Kim Dickens), Nick (Frank Dillane), and Alicia (Alycia Debnam-Carey) by adding on several intriguing and excellently acted new characters, namely the Otto clan: Jeremiah (superbly played by veteran Dayton Callie) and his 2 sons Jake (well played by Sam Underwood) and Troy (brilliantly performed by 'Teen Wolf' alum Daniel Sharman). Also, the show brought back a fan favorite character Daniel (excellently essayed once again by Ruben Blades) and adding in a couple of new strong characters in Lola (wonderfully played by Lisandra Tena) and Efrain (winningly played by TV vet Jesse Borrego), both connected to Daniel's subplot. Additionally, connected to the Otto subplot is the new character Walker (excellently played by Michael Greyeyes). Also returning are fan faves Ofelia (strongly played by Mercedes Mason) and Victor Strand (charmingly played by Colman Domingo) and an new character Dante (well played by Jason Manuel Olazabal).The FTWD writers really stepped up their game in Season 3. The writing was spare, believable, and character based, very much akin to the writing in the highly underrated Season 1. There wasn't a single episode that felt like a waste of time or filler. And everything really came together for an exciting 2-hour season finale, perhaps the first time where both hours of the 2-hour presentations were equally strong and not one clearly better than the other. And yet another great character was introduced in the finale, in the form of Proctor John (superbly played by Ray McKinnon). The casting for Season 3 was really spot on. The overarching plot of Season 3 is the Clark clan reuniting as Nick is reunited with his mother and sister in 3x01 and, unfortunately, Travis dies at the beginning of 3x02, but not before the family runs into a new enemy in the psychotic Troy Otto (the aforementioned Sharman in a season stealing performance), who is leader of a group of faux-military group "experimenting" on innocent people trying to figure out the turning patterns into the infected. The Clarks are rescued by Troy's older brother Jake and they all transport to the Otto family ranch, where the bulk of Season 3 takes place. The first half of Season 3 involves a range war between the Otto ranch residents and Walkers' people, who are held up at the local Indian reservation. Walker claims that Jeremiah's family stole their land and so Madison inserts herself smack dab in the middle of it in order to leverage control and a place that she and her kids can settle down on. Meanwhile, Strand is out on his own after getting kicked out of the hotel that he stayed in Season 2 finale and runs into an old associate Dante who controls a dam and acts as dictator as to who will get water in the community. Eventually, Daniel returns in 3x04, arguably best of the season, and has escaped the house fire from back in mid-Season 2 and gets saved and treated by a local homeless man Efrain and his friend Lola, who works for Dante at the dam. Thus, the genesis of all stories eventually converging in the second half of the season. During the season, some unlikely alliances take form: Madison-Jeremiah, Madison-Troy, Nick-Troy, Alicia-Jake (not really unlikely as Alicia takes up with every new hot young guy that pops up), Madison-Walker, Ofelia-Walker, Daniel-Strand. The writing really did a strong job of making all these interactions engrossing and entertaining. Like I stated, there were so many new strong characters added and the writing got so much better, the show had nowhere to go but up. The 2-hour finale was amazing, with Proctor John the driving force, and leaves on an astounding cliffhanger making me relish the return in Season 4, something I didn't think possible going into Season 3.

history.title: Diary of a Wimpy Kid: The Long Haul
history.text: THIS blu-ray come with the UV code for this film as well as the original 2010 movie. Good continuation of a really funny kids franchise. I think the story was very funny. Lot's of good comedy. A decently endearing story of a typical pre-teen boy trying to meet a youtuber. So that makes it a little more modern than the original trilogy. There was definitely some humor hidden in there for the adults watching it, including a hilarious reference to the classic film Psycho. As far as the cast. I think the New Wimp (Jason Drucker) did a very good job in the lead role. His timing and facial expressions, as well as physical acting was right on. The parents where parents, probably nothing special there. If they could have gotten the original parents back that would have been nice. Rowley was only in one or two scenes, so not much to mention there. The actor who plays the New Rodrick (Charlie Wright) did a good job being the low-IQ clueless older brother. His casting did cause controversy with fans, because he doesn't look that much like Drucker. However, if memory serves (the original Rodrick) Devon Bostick (who is now 25 and aged out of the role) did not look much like Zachary Gordon (the original Greg). Speaking of Zachary Gordon. Fans were also (strangely) upset that he did not reprise his role as the WIMPY KID regardless of the facts that he is now 19 years old, has a very husky deep adult voice, is in college, and clearly hits the gym on a regular basis and does a lot of weight lifting. Overall this movie was very funny and very fun, and has a lot of redeeming qualities. The story is fun. The acting is solid. The direction is as well. 9/10

history.title: The Hammer
history.review_title: The Kind of Movie that Studios Could Make Money on if They Still Made Them
history.text: It's not a big-budget film, but it's got a lot to offer content-wise. Kinda-sorta it's romantic comedy, but Carolla's artistic style seems to emphasize the process of achievement as an underdog, such that the "coming out a winner" is the "getting the girl" rather than actual winning the heart of a woman. This style element didn't harm my ability to enjoy the film since the romance is symbolic more than a driver of plot. Carolla is rightly celebrated for his rags-to-riches fame in his personal life, so it suits him to make stories surrounding the kinds of trials that have carried him to the success everyone wants. As a native of the area where this film is shot, I appreciated the Hollywood/Glendale locations. It established an important feel to the film, and cements Carolla's brand. The Oswoldo character is of tremendous value comedically, and functions not unlike Pedro in Napoleon Dynamite. However, his overly thick accent may frustrate some viewers. It's intentional, of course, to have Oswoldo barely able to communicate in English à la Manuel in Fawlty Towers. Since there was likely no budget for dialogue replacement, the ideal level of unintelligibility may not have been achieved. Watch Road Hard if you enjoyed this. Familiar themes for Carolla fans and just the thing to watch on a plane.

history.review_title: A Lot of Well-Showcased Comedic Talent Paint a Punishing Portrait of Success
history.text: I saw this film at its Hollywood premiere. I was stunned by how much I loved it and am surprised people strongly prefer The Hammer. I felt an emotional sophistication and performance quality that surprised and delighted me. The film will resonate instantly with corporate types who have to travel all the time and with everyone who's tired of beating themselves to a pulp trying to get ahead. To comment on details, I 'm utterly repulsed by Adam smoking, but showing him as a smoker allows for some nearly archaic humor which I valued.

history.title: Midnight
history.review_title: Amateurish, murky, boring, badly-scored, poorly acted, phoned in junk. And boring-- I mentioned boring, right?
history.text: After hearing Sam Sherman mention John Russo's Midnight on my umpteenth viewing of another movie released by Independent -International, I decided to grab a copy at what seemed like a bargain price. I'm staggered by how amateurish it is. Aside from Lawrence Tierney (who is terrible) the other actors don't seem to be trained professionals. It seems as though absolutely no effort was expended making this mess. The opening scene, featuring children who are clearly dressed in late 70s clothes, turns out to be a flashback from decades earlier. The female lead-- in her first scene I thought she was a boy (the haircut, clothes, and schlubby body language don't help). Not only does it compare poorly with similar, modern films made by complete amateurs at a fraction of the cost, but this worthless, boring waste of time is especially disappointing in that it was made by one of the men behind Night if the living Dead at the end of a decade that gave us Texas Chainsaw and Last House on the Left. I'm amazed even Sam Sherman thought it was worth releasing, and it wound up in Lion's Gate's clutches. The DVD opens with their logo, giving it a slight air of legitimacy. Until the movie starts, anyway.

history.review_title: Quality low budget production values ruined by non-actor cast
history.text: When this movie started I was really rooting for it. The opening sequence plays out well and there's a lit more attention to detail than in 90 percent of the low-budget videos I watch on Amazon. But the "performances" by the cast made the movie unbearable and I just could not finish it. Amateur actors don't necessarily ruin a movie-- many people have natural charisma onscreen that makes up for their lack of acting experience. Unfortunately, that's not the case here. I'm giving this 2 stars because of the strong opening and because I feel a little guilty quitting before the halfway mark.

history.title: The Unseen [Blu-ray] (1981)
history.text: What on EARTH are you people talking about? Are there TWO movies called The Unseen with Barbara Bach? Because the one I saw was a pleasantly-photographed story about a woman whose husband is an injured football player who may never play again. Their relationship is endangered because the husband (well played by Doug Barr) is apparently feeling sorry for himself and taking it out on Barbara Bach. Bach is a reporter and while covering a news story, she and her photographer (and another woman) wind up staying at the house of a mildly creepy couple. Something crawls through the ventilation and grabs Bach's two buddies in the most tedious and unscary scenes you could imagine. The film has no atmosphere and no tension, except perhaps over whether Bach will go through with a planned abortion. And at the climax, when Bach is crawling around a basement that's better-lit than my living room, we at last see the horror! What could the hideous cellar dwelling mutant be? Why it's Stephen Furst! And he's ADORABLE! A masterpiece of boredom!

history.title: Feeders / Among Us
history.review_title: Among Us is every movie all in one!
history.text: Feeders/Among Us 2-movie DVD review: Feeders is typical Polonia Bros vanity project (John even co-stars) no budget junk, but with nifty alien puppet monsters. Among Us is actually entertaining-- it's a horror movie and a Mockumentary and a comedy and a romance, and if it had had a more polished script, tighter editing, and slightly more professional (or better directed) actors, it would actually be a pretty neat little picture. But it's still a Polonia Bros movie. Watching it, you'll roll through two or three scenes going "you know, this isn't bad" and then BAM something will happen to remind you you're still stuck in Poloniaville. Which is not to knock the brothers-- their movies, whatever they lack, roll along and deliver at least the basic requirements of the kind of movies that they are. The main cast is certainly game (John Polonia's in it but has very few lines) and there are lots of great in-joke references to comics and movies too. Just kinda frustrating to see Among Us and think... If only they'd spent a little more time and effort...

history.title: Doctor Who: The Dominators (Story 44)
history.text: Everyone has their least favorite Dr. Who story, and The Dominators is mine. Because of the popularity of Patrick Troughton, and the scarcity of complete surviving Troughton stories, Dominators gets a kind of a free pass with fans. And that's OK, but a casual fan could be mislead by the reviews for this story and wind up buying something that could put them off Troughton's era, or 60s Who in general. The truth is, The Dominators has nothing going for it, other than five more episodes of Patrick Troughton's wonderful performance. Watching paint dry would be like a ride on the outside of a rocket compared to sitting through these 5 mind-numbingly dull, mostly poorly acted, indifferently directed episodes. The Quarks are terrible. They are short, barely mobile, unintelligible, and look like beat-up second hand furniture. Literally any other Troughton story would be a better choice for a casual fan looking to sample some of Peerless Pat's era.

history.text: I thought "Hey I have nothing else to watch (which I did), this has the guy from Breaking Bad from it (barely) and seemed to go under the radar (for good reason) why not?" I don't know what I expected. There were 3 moments I was beating the remote against my head at the stupidity of it: *SPOILER ALERT* (which I'm just trying to spare you the pain) First Face Palm: When they dropped off the Navy Seals in a jungle to find a lost Submarine, which after walking about 100 ft and finding the back end with the huge propeller it zooms out to show the 3 helicopters circling the OBVIOUSLY TALLER THAN THE TREES HUGE SUB. Second Face Palm: When they go to Nevada to check on the monster they locked up years ago in a mountain bunker. The marines are dropped of via helicopter (again) and kick down the Bunker door. only to see HALF THE MOUNTAIN BLOWN OUT and the HUGE monster heading towards the city THEY JUST CAME FROM. Oh and pulling out some binoculars for some stupid reason. Third Face Palm: When the tugboat going about 5-15 MPH carrying a nuke passes the Golden Gate Bridge by about 100 yards, with like 3 minutes left on the timer, a magical helicopter picks our "hero" up and clears the blast radius of a NUKE safely without the least turbulence. I don't think even MST3K could save this.

My friend kept telling me "Oh man it's so deep" "There is so many ways to look at it" "Blows your mind dude" I wanted to like it, I'm into interesting and unique movies, but about half way it completely lost me, my gf fell asleep, I didn't really care enough to find out what was going on, and just wanted it to be over with so I didn't feel like I threw away my money.

history.title: The Net
history.text: I caught this on TNT when I was in my teens and loved it. I really enjoy when a movie has a lead female role that's not a wimp. I also appreciate how they depict the Computer Guru's as every day (and in Sandra's case attractive) people, not obese basement dweebs. There are a few "what was that about" and a "seriously dude you didn't see that" moments but overall it's great. It's Enemy of the State meets 1995's "Hackers" meets Baywatch.

There is a very intelligent aspect this film has, that due to it's lack of popularity, went by unnoticed and undiscussed. Mission to Mars came out around that time, I guess they were just on a Mars streak. Both have the element of people being abandon on Mars, thought dead. This one threw a twist on it and was why I was renting it for a research article I was writing at the time. SPOILER - They sent bacteria to Mars after melting the Icecap, which contained mostly CO2, which helped create an atmosphere as the bacteria grew and created oxygen. Heck of a thought, why aren't we doing that...

Salma Hayek is one of the totemic figures of the 20th and 21st centuries. She is ageless. In this film, she portrays a healer in California who truly feels other people's pain. She is from Mexico, and in her contacts with Caucasians she is constantly belittled and condescended to. By chance, she is stranded at the lavish home of the mother of one of her clients and is invited to stay to dinner. The guest of honor, a real estate magnate and big game hunter, played by John Lithgow, is abrasive, abusive, combative, and all around hateful. During dinner, Beatriz does all she can to represent the need for healing, saving the earth, caring for others, and refraining from destruction. As a result, she is banished to the guest room. While sequestered, she makes an internet search of the mogul and finds her worst suspicions confirmed. The rich guests continue to amuse themselves downstairs. Beatriz makes one last appearance. In an alcohol- and marijuana-fueled speech, she compassionately and empathetically tells the man how his company ruined her town, threw people out of work, and destroyed the environment. Rather than spoil the ending, I will say that the film draws on magical realism and spiritualism. The photography is excellent. The music carries the mood without being intrusive. "Beatriz" was released this year and will probably win many awards.

When a riot breaks out, it is the producer who risks his own life to rescue the child of a local woman. The extras in the film the outsiders are making are recruited for $2 a day. They are so poor that any amount is riches to them. The stand-out actor is one of the locals, who becomes involved in protesting the water takeover. Chilling and enlightening.

It is an interesting story using Sharpe's early life in an orphans workhouse, the bitterness between him and his wife and her lover, and several characters from previous stories to make a fine tale. Although there is less action and more conniving than in previous episodes and the enemies are Sharpe's own countrymen instead of the French, I feel it fits well into the Sharpe series. The second disk, "Sharpe's Waterloo", is an excellent adaption of the book considering the vastness of the story's scope, although for those who haven't read the book Jane's fate will not be quite so fitting. My kids were excited to watch this but after a while one of them started reading a book and another started playing with something else. A voiceless option would let kids use their imagination about what is happening. Compare this to Disney's Dinosaur or the Korean Dino King. history.title: Innocent Bystanders
history.text: Innocent Bystanders is one of those spy films from the 1970s that hitched onto the coattails of the popular James Bond movies. Stanley Baker is both believable and poignant as a washed-up spy who’s been replaced by the next generation of British agents. Baker’s character was also been tortured on his last mission and has lost more than just a step. The movie becomes his quest for redemption. Can he step up and become the man he once was? While the movie obviously did not have the largest of budgets, its scenes ring true. Geraldine Chaplin is gorgeous as Baker’s love interest, and the all the actors turn in credible performances, especially Baker, who was an accomplished actor. The movie is well worth seeing if you’re a fan of those old spy flicks.

history.title: Bret Maverick: The Complete Series
history.text: Maverick didn't come there to lose, as Ed Bruce sang in the theme song. This reprisal of Garner's original western hero may have lasted only one season, but it was a very entertaining show. Garner brought along a few members Casting singer Ed Bruce as the co-star was a brilliant move. Bruce proved to be a fairly good actor and was the perfect foil to Garner's portrayal of the iconic Bret Maverick. While the episodes all take place in or around the town, as opposed to the perambulating in the original series, this suited the new format of a semi-retired Maverick who wanted to settle down and relax. It was unfortunate that the show was canceled after one season, despite good ratings. Garner's former Maverick co-star, Jack Kelly, who guest-starred on Rockford, made a surprise appearance at the end of the last episode, and was set to resume his role as Brother Bart had the show been renewed. As it stands, the series wraps things up effectively in the last episode, giving the feeling of closure that gives the reader the feeling of having completed a good novel. Garner would go one to play Mel Gibson's father in the movie version of the original series a few years later. He was a wonderful actor and projected authenticity and charm into every role he played. Do yourself a favor and get this complete series package and watch it over the course of a few days. It's to be savored, like a fine wine.

history.title: Zotz!
history.text: Zotz is a typical 1960's comedy that was well done for its time. The hero of the movie is eccentric college professor, Tom Poston, and he finds an ancient coin that gives him supernatural powers. Written during the height of the Cold War, the patriotic message might seem a bit dated today, but the comic situations still ring true. Poston uses the coin to thwart the Commies, as well as his nemesis, a bombastic colleague played by Jim Backus. The special effects are crude compared to today's CGI wonders, but the enthusiasm of the actors, doing so much with so little, carries the show. If you like period pieces from the 60's, you'll like Zotz.

history.title: Mr. Ricco
history.text: This one's for Dean Martin fans only. The quality is pretty low, and the movie has the look of a made-for-TV production. The plot is totally ridiculous. Made in the early 1970's, it was obviously trying to capitalize on the emerging "Blaxplotation" trend, with bad guy, white racist cops and thugs doing all the criminal work. Dino is rather miscast as a crusading attorney who gets a guilty man off, and runs afoul of the resentful cops. it stretches credulity that his best friend, played by Eugene Roche (probably best remembered for his dishwasher soap commercials), is a high ranking police detective. . Thalamus Rasulala and Philip Thomas (later of Miami Vice) play a black radicals, and gorgeous Denise Nicholas (Room 222) provides some "eye-candy" scenes. Dino has a knock-down, drag-out fight with Rasulala that isn't half bad, by professional wrestling standards,that is. Martin was a professional boxer before he entered show business, but he'd obviously lost his moves. Dino was at the end of the resurgence of his career when he made this one, and sort of sleepwalks through the role. He just looks plain tired. The ending is so far fetched and ridiculous that it borders on being a parody. It's too bad this marked the final leading movie role for Dino, because it was not a good way to go out. None of the Rat Pack really did well in their later choices of movie roles, and Martin's best role was playing himself on his variety show. This one is for hard core Dean Martin fans only.

history.title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
history.text: This was the second, and perhaps the best, of the Holmes movies featuring Basil Rathbone as Sherlock Holmes. Like its predecessor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, the movie is set in Victorian times, rather than the later Rathbone movies that updated Holmes and Watson to the Twentieth Century. Nigel Bruce pays Dr. Watson with a vigor and not for the comic relief, as he did in the later films with Rathbone. The quality of the print is beautiful, although not as beautiful as gorgeous Ida Lupino, who plays a young lady who is stalked by a killer. Toss in some dastardly plans by the redoubtable Professor Moriarty (George Zucco) and you have a perfect Holmes mystery. The best part of this movie is Rathbone's peerless performance. After watching this one, you'll have no doubt whom the best movie Holmes was. One of the best things about owning a DVD version is optional commentary that can be turned on. Watch the movie for the entertainment first, and then watch it again while listening to the commentary. This is a must for any fan of the world's most famous detective.

history.title: Panic in Year Zero (1962)
history.review_title: Put it in a Time Capsule
history.text: Made in the early 1960's, Panic in the Year Zero was a product of the Cold War hysteria that once gripped the nation. The movie, which starred and was directed by Milland, raises some thought provoking questions on how society might collapse in the face of a nuclear attack. The acting is adequate, but the movie had a very low budget and the black-and-white production looks like it was completed in about a week. It's an interesting glimpse of the mindset that dominated the country back then. It was made and released around the time of the Cuban Missile Crisis, so it remains an informative glimpse of the times back then. It also has some unintentional laughs as Milland argues with a gas station owner who has increased the price of the gasoline above the listed 35 cents a gallon. It belongs in a time capsule.

history.title: Larry McMurtry's Streets Of Laredo
history.review_title: Depressing Story Peppered With Gratuitous Violence
history.text: Streets of Laredo has a depressing story peppered with gratuitous violence. I was a long-time James Garner fan and bought the DVD primarily because it was one of his last roles. The quality of the DVDs was fair, although I did notice a bit of skipping here and there. The main problem I had with this one stemmed from the turgid story which rambled on and on. The novel upon whichit was based was over 500 pages long. This one should have been condensed into a two hour movie. If you do buy it, be prepared to be shocked by numerous scenes of exceptional brutality and get ready for a rather depressing story line. While it could be argued that this was probably a very realistic depiction of the actual West, there are some glaring historical misrepresentations in the plot. Judge Roy Bean, the famous, self-appointed hanging judge, is murdered in this mini-series, which was historically inaccurate. Gunslinger John Wesley Hardin is also depicted as presiding over a lawless town, which is another inaccuracy. Harden was actually imprisoned during the time depicted in the mini-series. All things considered, I found Steets of Laredo very disappointing. It crawls along at a snail's pace, with scenes of gratuitous violence that do little to enhance the story. Not only does it fail to be engaging, but the convoluted plot is anathema to the typical western. It tries to touch upon the idea of how legends were created, but the anticlimactic ending is overly long and so flawed that it robs the audience of any catharsis. The violence is equally disturbing, and the whole thing does not make for good entertainment, in the western tradition or otherwise. The "hero’s journey." a staple of the western genre, is not utilized, in favor of a depiction of a bunch of flawed individuals stumbling through the overwrought and preposterous plot, and punctuated with scenes of exceptional brutality. It might be argued that this is how it really was, but that’s not what the western genre is all about. Give me Louis L’Amour anytime.

history.title: Flesh and Bone [DVD]
history.text: Except for getting to see a lot of gorgeous Meg Ryan in various stages of undress, this one doesn't have much to offer in the way of entertainment. It's a rather depressing two hours of watching a bunch of losers stumble through a series of missteps to a confusing and unsatisfying climax. The plot doesn't really make much sense and has little cohesion. It's strung together by a crime committed by James Caan, who stumbles through the movie as a plot device, and witnessed by the Dennis Quaid character (Caan's son) as a boy. The screenwriter then strings together a series of unrelated and rather odd events until Caan once again shows up unexpectedly to set up the violent climax that is ludicrously overdone and depends upon the audience accepting some far fetched coincidences. All of the actors are usually first rate, but they're sleepwalking through their roles. The plot is so strained that it barely makes sense.

history.title: Bearcats! The Complete Series
history.text: Bearcats was a short-lived TV series of the early 70's starring rugged Rod Taylor. Dennis Cole portrayed Taylor's partner, a white man raised by the Indians. Although the series was moderately entertaining with a lot of small screen action, it's not hard to see why it was quickly canceled. The writers set the series in 1914, but were very careless about the plots. Anachronisms are prevalent from the onset, featuring tanks and aircraft that weren't invented until several years later. Although Taylor was a real pro, the scripts didn't give him much to work with, and acting was never Cole's strong suit. There is one interesting pairing of Taylor and muscleman actor, William Smith, where the two he-men get to resurrect their formidable pairing as adversaries as they did in the movie version of Darker Than Amber. The quality of the DVDs is good, but also a bit disappointing. The pilot episode, "Powderkeg," is not included in this collection, although it purports to be the "complete series." It's an interesting bit of nostalgia, but also a bit incomplete without "Powderkeg." I'd have to say it's somewhat of a misfire.
